newsitem.title: JAPAN: Australia PM pledges reform, seeks more investment.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM pledges reform, seeks more investment.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday assured Japan of his government's commitment to carrying out much-needed economic reforms, in a campaign to lure more investment from his nation's biggest trading partner.

In a speech to business executives in Tokyo, Howard said Australia would strive to reform its industrial relations system to ensure a more effective labour market, while taking steps to make its business infrastructure more cost-effective.

"I believe that these reforms will reduce the costs of doing business in Australia. They will make Australia more competitive and a more attractive partner for Japan and for your companies and institutions," Howard said.

Howard arrived in Japan on Wednesday for a four-day visit after winding up a three-day tour of Indonesia. It is his first major Asian tour as prime minister and has been closely watched as a key barometer as to whether his coalition government born in March will be less committed to Asia than its predecessor.

"The purpose of my visit is to assure you that my government is committed to advancing Australia's partnership with Japan. I see a dynamic partnership as serving Australia's and Japan's needs well into the next century. I also see it as making a crucial contribution to the prosperity and the stability of our region," Howard said.
Japan is the third-largest foreign investor in Australia. In 1995, Australia was the fourth-largest destination in the world for Japan's direct foreign investment, he said.
Bilateral trade between Australia and Japan was worth A$29.1 billion (US$23.2 billion) in the fiscal year to June 1995.

Howard painted a rosy economic picture of his country, saying that it would grow faster than any member of the Group of Seven (G7) countries in the next 18 months, with inflation expected to fall to around two percent by mid-1997.
But he added that his government also inherited an economy with some pressing structural problems.
"The most important are the problem of national savings, the lack of flexibility and competitiveness of Australia's labour market, and the constraints on small business," the prime minister said.
"If these problems are not addressed, growth in Australia will not reach its full potential, and we will not be able to reduce unemployment," he added.

He said his government's first priority has been to get its budget in order. "Increased national saving would help fund investment, reduce pressure on the current account deficit and interest rates, and enable Australia to sustain higher rates of economic and employment growth," he said.
Howard is due to meet meet Emperor Akihito and Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday.

Howard said he would like to discuss with Hashimoto how to consolidate the role of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum at the November APEC summit meeting at Subic Bay in the Philippines.

Australia, known as a strong advocate of liberalisation in the Asia-Pacific region, wants Japan to further liberalise and deregulate its market for agricultural products where Australia has an export interest.
"There are still areas where we would like to see further liberalisation and deregulation in Japan, including in the agricultural sector," he said.
